1.1: 1.1 I made a discourse. That is, I wrote: for to write is to work. Or he says this because by his deeds he deserved to be the writer of the Gospel. I made. The whole book of the Gospel is called one discourse, because it has one meaning; or the singular is put for the plural. The Gospel is good tidings, by which are announced rest after labor, a kingdom after servitude, life after death. Of all things. Of the words and deeds of Christ which he judged worthy of his office or suited to his dispensation. Theophilus. Theophilus is the same as friend of God, or lover of God: and if you are a friend of God, it is written to you. What Jesus began to do. From the baptism of John, in which Jesus was baptized, until the day on which he was taken up into heaven: for Luke wove together the discourses of that whole time, who at the end of the Gospel wrote thus: When he had blessed them, he departed from them and was carried up into heaven. To do. He establishes or instructs a good teacher, who does what he teaches.
1.2: 1.2 Commanding the apostles to preach the Gospel through the Holy Spirit, through whom the Gospel was preached, because he inspired the words and gave confidence. Or, commanding through the Holy Spirit, that is, what the Son commands, the Holy Spirit also commands. Or, he commanded on account of the Spirit, because he would not have commanded unless the Spirit were about to come. He chose. This turns to the praise of the apostles, whose acts he proposes to write. Taken up. Taken up by the Godhead, or taken up by a cloud, as a true man.
1.3: 1.3 Alive. A living and real body, not a phantasm, which the apostles also recognized as most familiar. Or alive, because he was living after death. Or alive, that is, no longer to die. Through days. Yet he did not appear to them for forty continuous days: for John says that four other days intervened after the day of the resurrection. After these he appeared again for forty: because he had been dead for forty hours, for forty days he confirms that he lives. And the forty can be understood as a type of the present age, in which Christ dwells in the Church: or because man, made up of four elements, is instructed against transgression of the Decalogue.
1.4: 1.4 Eating with them. He proclaims the signs of a true body, because he proved that he had risen not by one sense of the body, but by sight, hearing, touch, by appearing, speaking, eating together. The promise, which he promised through Joel, as is found in what follows: and although made by Christ, yet it will be fulfilled by the Father. Or it is called the Father's, because it is promised in his Word, that is, Christ.
1.5: 1.5 That John. BEDE. When the Lord said: That John baptized with water, but you, etc., down to what did not happen in the baptism of John. Baptism is given in two natures, namely bodily and spiritual: because the man who is baptized consists of two things, namely body and soul, yet there is one baptism, as there is one man. But you, etc. When Peter denied him, the apostles had not been baptized; not with water, but with the Spirit: for after the resurrection it was said: But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit. For they had not yet been confirmed by the resurrection of Christ and the sending of the Spirit. But as circumcision was not necessary for the righteous before it was commanded to Abraham and his posterity, so after the sacrament of the New Testament, that is baptism, was given in place of circumcision by the Lord saying: Unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Spirit John 3, etc., it is certain that no one belongs to the body of Christ unless he is baptized, except those to whom martyrdom is reckoned in place of baptism. Again, it is written when Paul was baptized: and it is not written when the other apostles were baptized: but we ought to understand that they were baptized because of that saying: Unless a man be born again, etc.
1.7: 1.7 It is not for you to know. He does not say, it will not be, but it is not: noting that they are still weak, and therefore not fit to know the secret. But when he says: It is not for you to know, he shows that he himself knows, to whom belong all things that are the Father's, but it is not expedient for them to know, but that they should live as if to be judged every day. Which the Father. The time of that kingdom, he says, is so secret that it lies open only to the knowledge of the Father, but you shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit, so that what you cannot do because of the weakness of the flesh, you may be able to do by the power of the Holy Spirit. In his own power. He said this as a true man, excusably, but there is only one power of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit: the Son also is the power of the Father.
1.8: 1.8 But you shall receive. The knowledge of the times is taken away, but the divine help they need is supplied: in the same way, when something is taken from children, something else is given so that they are not utterly saddened. Of the Holy Spirit coming upon you. When the Spirit comes upon you, he will not bring the kingdom of Israel, or the kingdom of God in Israel, as you suppose, but will furnish you the power of bearing witness about me, and the time of that kingdom is so far off that first the fame of the Gospel runs not only through Jerusalem, but through all the borders of Judea and Samaria, and even around to the ends of the world. In Jerusalem and in all Judea. The sequence of order is preserved in the names of the places: after Jerusalem comes the nearest province, Judea, to which Samaria is joined by its situation, then the communion of all the earth is added. In Jerusalem. Mystically: in the vision of peace, in the confession of the true faith: in the keeping of God's commandments: and he foretold that they would preach among those who have made themselves strangers to the land, through whom, like the spokes of a wheel from the middle of the earth where he wrought salvation, spiritual grace and saving doctrine flowed down through the whole world.
1.9: 1.9 And when he had said these things. Mark relates it differently, saying: And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven Matt. 28. But because Luke added more significantly: When he had said these things, he was lifted up, he shows that the Lord ascended to heaven when those words which he had recalled were completed.
1.11: 1.11 Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking up to heaven? In whom the understanding ought to be more prudent, because the Galileans excelled the other Jews in wisdom. Or, Galileans are changeable, because through the instability of their mind they will forget the precepts of God.
1.12: 1.12 Then they returned, etc. The return of the apostles from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem signifies the Church, which, ascending from the active life to the contemplative, descends again into the active way of life. For the Mount of Olives was called by the ancients the mount of three lights: namely of the lamp shining forth from the temple, and of the sun rising on the other side, and of the natural light of the oil on the mountain itself: which three agree with perfection, on account of the light of the divine Word shining from the Church, on account of the brightness of the sun of justice, on account of the radiance of a pure conscience.
1.13: 1.13 And when they had entered. In the Greek it is put thus: When they had entered the city, they went up to the upper room, where Peter was staying, etc. In the Greek the order of the names is thus: Peter and Andrew, James and John, Simon Zelotes and Judas of James. Upper room, etc. BEDE. It is a place on the upper level, signifying that, lifted from the earth, they climb to the heights of knowledge and virtue. The upper room is called the third story, a figure of charity built upon faith and hope. For charity is poured forth in our hearts by the Spirit. Peter and John. Peter is put first, because he is prince and shepherd. Peter and John are rightly put first, who ran together to the tomb, because they loved more than the rest. The first (if it is right to say so) loved more than the rest: the other Jesus loved most. The list of the apostles is given so that no false ones outside these may be received: and the places of each are set down equally, the grades of merit making distinctions. These are the twelve sons of Jacob; the twelve springs of the desert, which Israel found in Elim; the twelve loaves of proposition; the twelve stones on the garment of the high priest; the twelve signs of the zodiac; the twelve stones of the altar; the twelve stones raised from the Jordan; the twelve oxen under the bronze sea; the twelve stars in the crown of the bride; the twelve foundations; the twelve gates; the twelve months of the year; the twelve hours of the day; the twelve fruits of the tree of life. Zelotes. BEDE. Zelotes is the same who is called Canaanite in the Gospels. Cana is interpreted zeal. For he was from the village of Galilee where the Lord changed water into wine. He ruled the Church of the Jerusalemites after James his brother. With the son of perdition perishing, the number of the apostles remained incomplete; for like the moon the Church waxes and wanes: but old things pass away, and new are made.
1.14: 1.14 Mary, etc. The Virgin is distinguished from the women, although a woman is sometimes so called not for corruption but for sex. Behold, the beginning of the nascent Church is adorned with the flower of virginity. In the midst of the brethren. That is, of the sons, of whom one is the Father in heaven. Peter is said to have stood in the midst: as if condescending out of common compassion. This example is to be taken up by the shepherds of the Church. This number, one hundred and twenty, matches the age of Moses, so that as under this number, when Moses was dead, Jesus succeeded, who led the people into the promised land, so in the Church the primacy of Christ succeeded the old law, leading the true Israel to the kingdom of heaven.
1.18: 1.18 He possessed a field. Not that he possessed a field, but that the price of the field was his who sold the Lord of life. Having lost the land of the living, Judas possesses a field of blood and death, the eternal memory of his crime and his name. Yet he did not possess the field of the potter bought with the price of blood, for he straightway punished in himself the crime of betrayal, but possessed is said for caused to be possessed. Some ridiculously explain the field possessed by Judas as hell. Others think he possessed that field because he was buried in it with strangers. Bowels. The bowels, which are the seat of fraud, burst by so great a crime, could not hold themselves together. Rightly, however, the bowels are poured out through the seat of deceit, not through the place of the kiss, that is the mouth with which he kissed Jesus, though with a false surface, but through another part, in which was the poison of hidden malice.
1.19: 1.19 Of them, that is, of those dwelling in Jerusalem, because although both spoke Hebrew, yet the peculiarity of the language of the Jerusalemites differed from that of the Galileans, from whom the apostles were: which is shown in the Lord's passion, where even Peter, against his will, was betrayed by his speech as a Galilean.
1.20: 1.20 Let it be made desolate, and let there be none, etc. Until Matthias is chosen and taken in his place. Or, let Judas himself not be the one who dwells in it, but let another be taken in place of him who was judged unworthy of repentance.
1.23: 1.23 Two. Clement relates that these two who were set up for the lot of the apostolate were of the number of the seventy disciples. Who was surnamed. He lingers over the praise of Barnabas: because Matthew counts it for praise that he is chosen by lot. The praise of Barnabas is heaped up, lest he should seem to be rejected as unworthy: which was declared afterward; because he is ordained apostle of the Gentiles with Paul, reserved for that office. Justus. It is either Latin or Hebrew: and is interpreted sparing, or lifted up. And Matthias, who is interpreted given, or gift of God: to whom the gift of the apostolate was conferred by the Lord, or is interpreted cloth of God. Rightly, says Arator, he who was just is surpassed by the praise of men, for the little one.
2.1: 2.1 In the same place. That is, the upper room into which they had gone up. He who desires the Spirit, rising above the dwelling of the flesh by contemplation of the mind, treads it underfoot.
2.2: 2.2 From heaven. The Spirit is given from heaven, that God may be loved; on earth he is given, that the neighbor may be loved: for he was given twice after the resurrection to commend the two precepts of charity. A sound. The speech of tongues sounding from the mouths of the apostles can be called a sound. The Spirit. Before the passion the Spirit was given to the apostles for the grace of teaching and of healings; after the resurrection Jesus breathed on them and said: Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them John 20, etc. This gift he had earlier given to Peter alone: but, as is believed, it was then given by anticipation, now with the others by completion it is granted to Peter also: and the power of forgiving was given to those whom he was sending to the office of preaching. Mighty. By comparison with the earlier gifts the grace of the apostles is called mighty, or the Spirit came in the likeness of a mighty wind. The whole house. The Spirit is poured out on those sitting in one house, to commend the unity of the Church, in the upper room, as the third law begins. At the giving of the law the people stood far off for fear; here, at the coming of the Spirit, they were gathered into one out of love. Sitting. That what had been said to them might be fulfilled: Sit here in the city. Sitting is a sign of humility and steadfastness: a seat is prepared for the Holy Spirit in these, who rests upon the humble. GREGORY. The Spirit appeared in fire, but by himself, etc., down to hearts were taught both by voice and by sound.
2.3: 2.3 Parted. The dispersion of tongues happened at the tower, but what pride scattered, humility gathers again: in pride is dispersion, in humility concord comes about. Behold, the saying of the Lord is fulfilled, who said: I will not leave you orphans, but I will send the Spirit, the Paraclete John 14, who, as their advocate, spoke for them in all tongues. He who came for the Word brought tongues, for the tongue has kinship with the word, so that they cannot be separated from each other. So the Word of the Father, that is the Son, and the Holy Spirit are inseparable, indeed of one nature. As of fire. The Spirit likewise came in fire: because the Spirit purges, enlightens, kindles, burns sinners. For fire has four natures: it burns, purges, warms, illuminates. Similarly the Spirit burns away sins, purges hearts, shakes off torpor, lights up ignorance. Fire is incorporeal and invisible in its own nature; but when it takes up some body it is seen, appearing of different colors, because of the materials in which it burns. So the Spirit could not be seen except through the creatures in which he works.
2.4: 2.4 And they began. Behold the sign of fullness: a full vessel bursts forth. Fire in the bosom cannot be hidden. With various tongues. Because they spoke in all tongues, or, speaking in their own, that is the Hebrew tongue, they were so understood by all as if they were speaking in the language of each, according to the saying of the Prophet: In other tongues, and by other lips, I will speak to this people, etc.
2.5: 2.5 From every nation, etc. RABANUS. As if to say: Wherever they were born. The captivity, which took place under Antiochus not many times before, caused Jews to be born among all nations.
2.6: 2.6 Confounded. This confusion is set against the confusion of tongues, from which Babel got its name. So the humility of the apostles answers the pride of men. Each one. The tongues are all said to be seventy-two: whence the disciples of the second rank were chosen under this number, so that the number of the preachers might agree with the number of the tongues.
2.8: 2.8 We have heard. In this it was signified that the one Church would speak in the tongues of all nations. BEDE. The question is asked whether those who were speaking, etc., down to the miracle seemed to belong more to the hearers than to the speakers.
2.9: 2.9 Cappadocia, etc. These five provinces which are put after Judea speak Greek indeed: but from the custom of their country there is a diversity in sound. Whence the grace in the apostles was wonderful, which taught them not only the diversity, but also made in their speech the distance between the peculiarities in each of the languages, according to the number of the provinces.
2.10: 2.10 Strangers of Rome. In the Greek, sojourning Romans, that is, Jews who led a life of sojourning at Rome.
2.14: 2.14 Men of Judea. That is, there are two causes of prudence, namely that they are Jews, and that they dwell in Jerusalem, for which sobriety is fitting.
2.17: 2.17 I will pour out. By this word he shows the generosity of the gift, because the Spirit was to be given not, as formerly, only to prophets and priests, but to persons of both sexes everywhere without distinction. Of my Spirit. He has regard to the diverse gifts when he says this, but not to any lessening of the substance. Upon all flesh. Who is meant by all flesh he explains next in what follows: And your sons shall prophesy, etc. RABANUS. Upon all flesh, male and female, or circumcised and Gentile, according to the saying: There is neither male nor female, circumcision nor uncircumcision, Barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free Gal. 3. And they shall prophesy. The law and the prophets until John: from then the kingdom is preached. But it is one thing to prophesy of Christ, another to foretell and teach things to come.
2.19: 2.19 And I will give. Mystically, wonders in heaven are labors in the Church. Signs, on the earth. Vengeances, upon earthly men. Blood, in martyrdom. Fire, of the Gospel or of the Holy Spirit. Vapor of smoke, the compunction of the soul or heart. Wonders in heaven. For when Christ was born, a new star appeared; when he ascended the cross, the sun was darkened and the sky was covered with darkness. Blood. Not only of the wound, but also of sweat, when in prayer his sweat became like drops of blood, which is counted among the signs of the Godhead, because it is not found in human nature. Therefore it signifies that the whole world was to be washed with the blood of Christ, so that as the tabernacle had been consecrated with the blood of victims, so the faithful people might be dedicated with his blood: and that not only in Jerusalem would there be a place of prayer, but in every place of his dominion the elect might lift up hands to the Lord in prayers. Vapor of smoke. Namely the vapor of compunction and of tears. For as smoke comes from fire, so compunction comes from the ardor of the Holy Spirit. The sun shall be turned, etc. This is believed to have been done partly in the passion of Christ and partly to come before the day of judgment. For then the sun was darkened, but the moon turned to blood could not appear to men: because then (as at the Passover) being fifteen days old, it had been hidden from human sight by the interposition of the earth during the day.
